facts.claim: Atlas of the Heart (2021) by Brené Brown maps 87 emotions and experiences, grouped into 13 'land masses' (Time).
Brown's team surveyed about 7,000 people over five years; on average people could name only three emotions as they were feeling them: happiness, sadness, anger.
Envy occurs when we want something that another person has. Looks, status and wealth are the big trio.
facts.source: Book definition via excerpt page; Time

facts.claim: Jealousy is when we fear losing a relationship, or a valued part of a relationship, that we already have. It involves three parties (you, the person you are close to, and the perceived rival).
Envy and jealousy sit in the 'Places We Go When We Compare' section, beside comparison, admiration, schadenfreude and freudenfreude.

Brown says she always thought resentment lived close to anger, but it turns out resentment is not part of the anger family; it is a function of envy. The idea came out of an interview with Marc Brackett.
Resentment involves feelings of unfairness or being treated unfairly, and can hide an unspoken need or an unfair balance.

rejected.claim: More than 50% of people use only three words (happy, sad, angry)
rejected.reason: Book/Time says 'on average people can identify only three emotions'; no 50% figure.

rejected.claim: Anger is alive/informative; resentment (kin) is 'dead' and drains energy; resentment resolved by letting go; 'forgiveness frees you not them'
rejected.reason: Not Brown's Atlas claim. Her claim: resentment is part of envy, not anger. Dropped.

rejected.claim: Envy should be read as 'I want that too' (not 'why is he so lucky'); the writer example about a friend's book
rejected.reason: Interpretive advice and example not found in sources; kept out of story, may appear only as a reader-side suggestion in the lesson/use cards.

rejected.claim: Naming emotions makes them manageable; 'you can't manage what you can't name'
rejected.reason: Not a quote found in sources; do not attribute.

1649.note: Envy (two parties, wanting what they have) vs jealousy (three parties, fear of losing a relationship).

1650.note: Rebuilt on Brown's actual claim: resentment belongs to envy, not anger. Old anger-alive/resentment-dead frame dropped. Medium confidence, secondary sources only.
